source_text: O sanitatem, o elegantiam disputantis! Non ideo, inquit, malum exortum est in homine, quia a Deo factum est, sed ideo quia de nihilo [n71] . Ostendimus iam acumen, quo vis maxima huic nihilo subrogata est; nunc illud admoneo, quod etiam superior conflictus fecit intellegi, nec primum malum peccantis fuisse voluntate susceptum, si illud nasci conditio venientis de nihilo stirpis exegit.
pass_a_gloss: O health, o elegance of the disputant! Not therefore, he says, did evil arise in the human, because it was made by God, but therefore because from nothing. We have already shown the sharpness by which a greatest force was subrogated to this nothing; now I advise that which even the earlier conflict made understood, that not even the first evil of the one sinning was taken up by will, if the condition of a stock coming from nothing demanded that it be born.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: What soundness! What elegance in a debater! ‘Evil arose in a human being,’ he says, ‘not because he was made by God, but because he was made from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48). We have already shown the sharpness by which immense power is assigned to this nothing. Now I point out what the preceding debate also made clear: not even the first evil was undertaken by the sinner’s will if the condition of an origin from nothing required its birth.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
